source_text: Veterem legem secundum Apostolum iustam et sanctam et bonam, custodientibus mandata sua ac per fidem iuste viventibus sicut Prophetis et Patriarchis omnibusque sanctis vitam potuisse conferre perpetuam
pass_a_gloss: that the old law, according to the Apostle just and holy and good, was able to confer everlasting life on those keeping its commandments and living justly through faith, as on the Prophets and Patriarchs and all the saints

lemmas.lexica: LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: The old law, which according to the apostle is just, holy, and good, was able to grant everlasting life to those who kept its commandments and lived rightly through faith, as the prophets, patriarchs, and all the saints did (Romans 7:12).

choices.why: Julian means Scripture's legal/authoritative witness, especially the divine Law as teacher of justice.
rejected: natural law (unless the sentence is philosophical)

choices.why: Paul in Julian's citations; keep Apostle not 'Paul' unless Paulus is written.
Opening fides promissionis is the pledge of a promise, not the theological virtue.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

bible_refs.note: Linked from Julian's wording or a clear allusion in the excerpt.

speaker: Julian and fellow bishops (Collective letter to Thessalonica, words preserved in Augustine, Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 2–4); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
